analogy.p: Imagine a pile of paperclips that each have one open end. Each paperclip is a monomer, and when they link together end to end they make one long chain, the polymer. Every single paperclip ends up in the chain and nothing falls off, just like addition polymerisation where there is no other product. The repeat unit is one paperclip in the chain. The analogy breaks down because real monomers do not have an open end drawn on them: it is the C=C double bond opening that makes the free bonds, and the real chain is held by covalent bonds, not by hooks.

bullets: **Monomer** = a small molecule that can join with many others to make a polymer (for addition polymers, a molecule with a **C=C** bond).
**Polymer** = a very large molecule made of many repeating units joined by covalent bonds; the atoms in the long chain are held together by strong covalent bonds.
**Polymerisation** = the reaction in which many monomers join together to form a polymer.
In **addition polymerisation** the monomers contain a C=C bond and join with **no other product** being formed.
Typical numbers: a polymer molecule may contain thousands of repeat units, which is why the formula is written with a letter **n**.
Examples to know: **poly(ethene)** from ethene and **poly(propene)** from propene (named in the AQA specification).
core.p: A **polymer** is a very large molecule made of many small repeating units joined together by covalent bonds. The small molecules that join up are called **monomers**, and the process of joining them is called **polymerisation**. In **addition polymerisation** the monomers simply add on to each other one after another, so the polymer contains every atom that was in the monomers and no other substance is made. Poly(ethene) is the standard example: thousands of ethene molecules join to make one enormous poly(ethene) molecule, which is the plastic used for carrier bags.

bullets: **Unsaturated** = contains a C=C double bond; **saturated** = only single C–C bonds.
Functional group of alkenes = **C=C**; the general formula of alkenes is **CnH2n** (ethene C2H4, propene C3H6).
One of the two bonds in the double bond **opens up**, so each carbon can make a new single bond to another monomer.
Because the double bond is reactive, ethene decolourises **bromine water**; this is the test for unsaturation.
Alkanes (e.g. ethane) cannot make addition polymers because they have **no C=C bond** to open.
Link to other topics: alkenes are made by **cracking** long-chain alkanes from crude oil, so crude oil is the raw material for many plastics.
core.h: Why alkenes can polymerise: the C=C functional group
core.p: Alkenes are **unsaturated** hydrocarbons: they contain at least one carbon–carbon **double bond** (C=C), which is their **functional group**. A functional group is the part of a molecule that gives it its characteristic reactions. The double bond is a pair of shared electron pairs between two carbon atoms, and one of those two bonds is easily broken, which leaves each carbon able to form a new bond to another atom. That is exactly what happens when alkenes react with bromine, hydrogen or steam in addition reactions, and it is also why alkenes are able to join to each other. Alkanes have only single bonds, are saturated, and cannot polymerise this way.

bullets: **Step 1:** each monomer has a C=C double bond.
**Step 2:** one bond of every C=C double bond breaks (the double bond 'opens'), leaving two free bonds on each monomer.
**Step 3:** the free bonds link to the neighbouring monomers, forming new **single** C–C bonds.
**Step 4:** this repeats thousands of times, producing a long chain: the **polymer**.
Only **one** product is made, the polymer; there is **no small molecule** given off.
Details of the conditions (for ethene, usually high pressure and a catalyst) are **not required** by AQA, but the idea of the double bond opening is.
core.h: Step by step: what happens in the reaction
core.p: Imagine a very large number of ethene molecules close together, with suitable conditions. In each molecule the double bond opens, so each of the two carbon atoms now has a free bond (a place to join). The free bond on one monomer then bonds to the free bond on the next monomer, and this repeats over and over, building a chain one monomer at a time. Because the bond that opened has been used to join monomers, the chain is held by single carbon–carbon bonds, and the final polymer contains no C=C bonds. Nothing is lost, so the total number of atoms in the polymer equals the total number of atoms in the monomers.

bullets: Equation for ethene: **n CH2=CH2 → (–CH2–CH2–)n** (the C=C on the left becomes a single bond on the right).
Equation for propene: **n CH2=CHCH3 → (–CH2–CH(CH3)–)n**.
Equation for chloroethene: **n CH2=CHCl → (–CH2–CHCl–)n**.
On the left each monomer is **separate**; on the right the polymer is **one molecule**.
The number of atoms is the same on both sides: addition polymerisation has **100% atom economy** (all reactant atoms end up in the useful product).
The **n** on the left means 'many molecules'; the **n** on the right means 'many repeat units'; they are the same number.
core.p: The word equation is: ethene → poly(ethene), and the symbol equation uses n to stand for the large number of molecules: n CH2=CH2 → (–CH2–CH2–)n. The letter n is a very big number (often thousands), so you must never replace it with a specific small number in an exam unless told to. The brackets show the **repeat unit**, and the subscript n shows it is repeated n times. The equation balances because n monomers each contribute C2H4, and the polymer contains n repeat units each of C2H4, so the atoms on both sides match exactly.

bullets: Draw **square brackets** (or round) around the repeat unit with a small **n** at the bottom right.
The bonds on each side must **cross the brackets**: these are the bonds to the next repeat units; do not leave them out.
The backbone of the chain is always **carbon atoms joined by single bonds**.
For an addition polymer the repeat unit has the **same atoms** as the monomer that made it.
The repeat unit is a **bit of the polymer**, not a separate molecule, so it is not a molecule that exists on its own.
A 'repeating unit' is the same thing as 'repeat unit' for this specification.
core.h: The repeat unit and the brackets
core.p: The **repeat unit** is the smallest group of atoms that is repeated again and again along the polymer chain. In diagrams it is drawn inside **brackets**, and the bonds at both ends are drawn so they **go through the brackets** to show that the chain continues in both directions. The repeat unit looks like the monomer but with the double bond turned into a single bond. For an addition polymer the repeat unit has the same atoms as the monomer, the carbon–carbon bond in the backbone is now single, and the two outer bonds (the ones which were part of the double bond) stick out of the brackets.

bullets: Rule: **poly(** monomer name **)**.
ethene → **poly(ethene)** (also called polythene), used for bags and bottles.
propene → **poly(propene)** (also called polypropylene), used for crates and ropes.
chloroethene → **poly(chloroethene)**, also known as PVC, used for pipes and window frames.
tetrafluoroethene → **poly(tetrafluoroethene)**, also known as PTFE, used for non-stick coatings.
To name the monomer from the polymer name, **remove 'poly' and the brackets**: poly(propene) → propene.
core.p: Addition polymers are named by putting **poly** in front of the name of the monomer, with the monomer name in brackets. So ethene gives poly(ethene), propene gives poly(propene) and chloroethene gives poly(chloroethene). The brackets are not essential for credit in most questions but they remove any doubt, especially for monomers that have long names. The name tells you the monomer, so from the name you can work out the monomer by simply removing the word poly.

bullets: **Step 1:** draw the monomer with the C=C in the middle and the other atoms above and below.
**Step 2:** turn C=C into a single **C–C** bond.
**Step 3:** add a bond going out from each of the two carbons (to join to the next units).
**Step 4:** put brackets across these two outgoing bonds and write **n** after the bracket.
Example, ethene: repeat unit **–CH2–CH2–** (H on each carbon).
Example, chloroethene: **–CH2–CHCl–** (the Cl stays on the second carbon).
Example, tetrafluoroethene: **–CF2–CF2–** (all four F stay on the carbons).
The backbone has exactly **two carbons per repeat unit** for these alkene monomers.
core.h: Drawing the repeat unit from the monomer
core.p: The method is the same every time. Draw the monomer so that the two carbon atoms of the C=C are side by side in a line, with all the other atoms or groups pointing up or down from them. Then change the double bond into a **single bond**, add a bond sticking out of each carbon on the outside, and draw brackets with n. Every atom or group that was attached to the two carbons of the double bond stays attached to the same carbon. For propene, which is CH2=CH–CH3, the CH3 group stays on the second carbon, so the repeat unit is –CH2–CH(CH3)–.

bullets: **Step 1:** find the repeating pattern in the chain and mark one repeat unit (two backbone carbons).
**Step 2:** redraw those two carbons with a **C=C** between them.
**Step 3:** keep all atoms or groups attached to those two carbons; remove the outgoing bonds and the brackets.
**Step 4:** name the monomer (an alkene, or a substituted ethene such as chloroethene).
Check: the monomer must contain **a C=C double bond**; if it does not, you have made a mistake.
Check the formula: the number of atoms in the repeat unit must equal the number in the monomer.
core.h: Working out the monomer from the polymer
core.p: Exam questions often show a section of polymer and ask for the monomer. The reverse method is to pick out one repeat unit, which for these polymers has two carbon atoms in the backbone, and then change the single bond between those two carbons back into a **double bond** and remove the two outgoing bonds. Everything else attached to the two carbons stays. Take care to choose the repeat unit with exactly two backbone carbons; choosing one carbon or four gives a wrong answer. If the polymer is drawn as a long section, check that you pick two carbons next to each other, and that the groups you include are the ones on those two carbons.

bullets: **Poly(ethene):** carrier bags, bottles, cling film (low-density types are flexible).
**Poly(propene):** crates, ropes, carpets, food containers.
**Poly(chloroethene) (PVC):** drain pipes, window frames, wire insulation.
**Poly(tetrafluoroethene) (PTFE):** non-stick coating on pans.
All these are made from **alkenes** (or substituted alkenes) with a C=C bond.
Different side groups (H, CH3, Cl, F) change **how the chains pack**, giving different properties.
core.h: Examples and uses of addition polymers
core.p: Many everyday plastics are addition polymers. Their properties depend on the groups attached to the carbon backbone, which is why different monomers give different plastics. Poly(ethene) is flexible and cheap, poly(propene) is stronger and stiffer so can be used for crates and ropes, poly(chloroethene) is rigid and hard-wearing and is used for pipes, and poly(tetrafluoroethene) is very slippery and unreactive so it is used for non-stick coatings. You do not usually have to learn properties and uses for this point, but knowing a few helps you answer context questions.

bullets: Mr of chloroethene C2H3Cl = 2 × 12 + 3 + 35.5 = **62.5**.
Mr of polymer = **n × Mr of repeat unit**, so n = Mr of polymer ÷ Mr of repeat unit.
Mass conserved: polymer mass = **sum of monomer masses** because nothing is lost.
**Atom economy** = Mr of desired product ÷ sum of Mr of reactants × 100; here 100%.
Contrast: **condensation polymerisation** loses a small molecule, so the polymer is lighter than the monomers.
core.h: No by-product: atom economy and mass
core.p: In addition polymerisation the polymer is the only product. This means all the atoms of the reactants appear in the product, so the **atom economy** is 100%, and the mass of polymer formed equals the total mass of monomer used (if the reaction is complete). The relative formula mass of the polymer equals n times the relative formula mass of the repeat unit, and the repeat unit has the same formula mass as the monomer. For example, ethene C2H4 has Mr = 28, so a poly(ethene) molecule made from 1000 monomers has Mr = 28 000.

bullets: Monomer (ethene) is a **gas**; polymer (poly(ethene)) is a **solid** because of larger intermolecular forces.
The polymer is **saturated**: it does not decolourise bromine water, but the alkene monomer does.
Strong covalent bonds along the chain make the polymer **strong and durable**.
Most addition polymers are **not biodegradable**, so they cause **waste disposal problems** in landfill.
Link: waste plastics can be recycled or burned for energy, (Using resources topic).
Link: thermosoftening polymers have weak forces between chains so they **soften on heating** (do not confuse with the covalent bonds along the chain).
core.h: Properties of the polymer compared with the monomer
core.p: The polymer has very different properties from its monomer. Ethene is a gas at room temperature but poly(ethene) is a solid, because the very long molecules have strong **intermolecular forces** between them (the forces get bigger as molecules get larger) and so a lot of energy is needed to separate them. The polymer chain has **no C=C bonds** left, so it is saturated and mostly unreactive, whereas the monomer reacts readily with bromine water. This is why plastics are useful for containers and pipes. The strong C–C bonds in the backbone also mean most addition polymers are **not biodegradable**.

bullets: Addition: monomers have a **C=C** bond; condensation: monomers have **two functional groups** (e.g. –OH and –COOH).
Addition: **one product** (the polymer); condensation: **polymer plus a small molecule** such as water.
Addition: **usually one monomer**; condensation (polyester): **two different monomers**.
Addition polymer repeat unit = **same atoms as the monomer**; condensation repeat unit has **lost atoms**.
Addition polymers have a **carbon-only backbone**; polyesters have **ester links** in the backbone.
Use the words **'functional group'** and **'repeating unit'** in explanations to match the specification.
core.h: Addition versus condensation, and the exam link
core.p: AQA wants you to be able to explain the principles of addition polymerisation using the **functional group in the monomer** (the C=C double bond) and the **repeating unit in the polymer**. Condensation polymerisation (triple science) is different because the monomers have two functional groups, usually two different monomers are involved, and a small molecule such as water is lost each time two monomers join. In addition polymerisation there is usually one type of monomer and nothing is lost. Be clear which kind is being asked about, because the same question stem ('explain how this polymer forms') needs very different answers.

exam: **State/name (1 mark):** give the name using the rule 'poly(' + monomer + ')', e.g. poly(propene).
**Draw the repeat unit (2 marks):** correct atoms in the brackets (1) and the outgoing bonds through the brackets plus n (1).
**Draw the monomer (1–2 marks):** C=C drawn with all the original atoms on the correct carbons; the monomer must have a double bond.
**Describe how an addition polymer forms (2–3 marks):** monomers contain a C=C double bond (1); double bond opens / breaks (1); many monomers join to form a long chain, no other product (1).
**Explain why alkenes can form polymers but alkanes cannot (2 marks):** alkenes have a C=C (1) which can open to form bonds to other molecules (1); alkanes are saturated/have no double bond.
**Command word 'Explain' (typical 3–4 marks):** each point needs a reason ('because the C=C double bond opens, so the monomers can join').
**Equation questions:** write n CH2=CH2 → (–CH2–CH2–)n, with brackets, with n on both sides.
**Calculation:** n = Mr of polymer ÷ Mr of repeat unit; show the working and units are not needed for Mr.
**Compare addition and condensation (triple):** use 'functional group', 'repeating unit' and 'small molecule lost'.
**6-mark questions:** organise as (1) what a monomer is, (2) double bond opens, (3) chain forms, (4) no other product, (5) example, (6) properties/uses.

mistakes.r: The monomer is ethene (an alkene with C=C); alkanes have no double bond to open.
mistakes.w: Writing that the polymer is made by 'joining ethane molecules'.

mistakes.r: In the polymer the carbon–carbon bond in the backbone is a **single** bond; the C=C has opened.
mistakes.w: Leaving the double bond in the repeat unit.

mistakes.r: The bonds at each end must cross the brackets to show the chain continues.
mistakes.w: Drawing the repeat unit without the outgoing bonds through the brackets.

mistakes.r: n is a very large number; write the subscript n after the bracket.
mistakes.w: Leaving out the n (or using a small number).

mistakes.r: In addition polymerisation the polymer is the **only** product.
mistakes.w: Saying water or another small molecule is made.

mistakes.r: For these monomers the repeat unit has the two carbons that were the C=C.
mistakes.w: Choosing four carbons or one carbon as the repeat unit.

mistakes.r: Every atom stays attached to the same carbon it was attached to in the monomer.
mistakes.w: Moving the CH3 or Cl to a different carbon or changing atoms.

mistakes.r: Poly(ethene) is a saturated molecule with no C=C.
mistakes.w: Saying the polymer is a mixture of different molecules or 'a big alkene'.

mistakes.r: Name from the monomer: ethene gives poly(ethene).

summary: AQA wants you to know that alkenes can be used to make addition polymers such as poly(ethene) and poly(propene): many small **monomer** molecules, each containing a **C=C double bond**, join together to make one very long **polymer** molecule with nothing else formed. You must be able to recognise addition polymers and monomers from diagrams, draw the **repeat unit**, name the polymer, and explain the idea using the functional group in the monomer and the repeating unit in the polymer. It matters because plastics are everywhere and this is the simplest way they are made.

terms.d: A small molecule that can join with many other small molecules to form a polymer.
A very large molecule made of many repeating units joined by covalent bonds.
A reaction in which many small molecules (monomers) join together to form a very large molecule (polymer).
Polymerisation in which monomers containing a C=C bond join together with no other product being formed.
A polymer made by addition polymerisation of monomers containing a C=C double bond.
A hydrocarbon containing a carbon–carbon double bond; general formula CnH2n.
Containing a C=C double bond so that more atoms can be added.
Containing only single carbon–carbon bonds; no C=C.
The group of atoms in a molecule that gives it its characteristic chemical reactions; in alkenes it is C=C.
The smallest group of atoms that is repeated along the polymer chain; shown inside brackets with n.
A very large number showing how many repeat units (or monomer molecules) there are.
The relative formula mass of the desired product divided by the total relative formula mass of all reactants, × 100.
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms; the bonds along the polymer backbone.
Forces between molecules; stronger for larger molecules, so polymers are solids.
Able to be broken down by microorganisms; most addition polymers are not.

worked.ans: n CH2=CHCH3 → (–CH2–CH(CH3)–)n ; repeat unit in brackets with bonds through the brackets and n at the bottom right.
worked.q: Draw the repeat unit of poly(propene) and write the equation for its formation. [3 marks]
steps: Propene is CH2=CH–CH3: the two carbons of the double bond are CH2 and CH(CH3).
Change C=C to C–C and add outgoing bonds: the repeat unit is –CH2–CH(CH3)–.
Put in brackets with n; balance with n molecules of monomer.

worked.q: A sample of poly(ethene) has a relative formula mass of 28 000. How many ethene molecules joined to make one molecule? (Ar: C = 12, H = 1) [2 marks]
steps: The repeat unit has the same Mr as the monomer, 28.

worked.ans: Ethene molecules each contain a C=C double bond (1). The double bond opens/one of the bonds breaks (1). The monomers join together by forming single bonds (1) to form a very long chain / polymer, poly(ethene), and no other product is formed (1).
